sections.title: What is AWS and Cloud Computing?
sections.content:
Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of computing resources — servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics, and intelligence — over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Instead of owning and maintaining physical data centers and servers, businesses rent access to these resources from a cloud provider like Amazon Web Services (AWS). This model eliminates the need to make large upfront capital expenditures (CapEx) and instead treats infrastructure as an operational expense (OpEx) that scales with usage.

Cloud services are typically categorized into three models. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) gives you the most control — you manage the OS, runtime, and applications while AWS manages the underlying hardware and virtualization (EC2 is IaaS). Platform as a Service (PaaS) abstracts the OS and runtime so you only manage your application and data (Elastic Beanstalk, RDS). Software as a Service (SaaS) delivers a fully managed application (think Gmail or Salesforce) where the provider manages everything.

AWS holds the largest share of the public cloud market (roughly 31-33% as of recent reports), ahead of Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. AWS launched in 2006 with just S3 and EC2, and now offers over 200 fully featured services. Key advantages businesses cite for moving to AWS include global reach, elasticity (scale up/down in minutes), managed services that reduce operational burden, a vast partner ecosystem, and a pay-per-use model that aligns costs directly with business activity.

sections.title: Regions and Availability Zones
sections.content:
An AWS Region is a geographically distinct area that contains multiple, isolated locations called Availability Zones. Each Region is a separate geographic area such as us-east-1 (Northern Virginia), eu-west-1 (Ireland), or ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). AWS currently operates 33+ Regions worldwide, with more being added regularly. Regions are completely independent from one another — a failure in one Region does not affect another.

An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more discrete data centers within a Region, each with redundant power, networking, and connectivity. AZs within a Region are interconnected via high-bandwidth, low-latency links but are physically separated by meaningful distances (often tens of miles) to protect against localized disasters. Every Region has a minimum of 3 AZs (for example, us-east-1 has 6 AZs: us-east-1a through us-east-1f). Designing your application to span multiple AZs is the foundation of high availability on AWS.

Edge Locations are endpoints used by Amazon CloudFront for content delivery — there are 400+ edge locations worldwide, far more than Regions. They cache content closer to end users to reduce latency. When choosing a Region for your workload, consider four factors: latency to your end users (pick geographically close), data residency and compliance regulations (GDPR requires EU data to stay in EU), service availability (not all services are in all Regions — always verify), and pricing (costs vary by Region, sometimes by 10-20%).
sections.codeExample:
# List all AWS Regions via CLI
aws ec2 describe-regions --query 'Regions[].RegionName' --output table

# List Availability Zones in a specific region
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'AvailabilityZones[].ZoneName' \
  --output table

# Region naming convention:
# us-east-1      → US East (N. Virginia) — oldest, most services
# us-west-2      → US West (Oregon)
# eu-central-1   → Europe (Frankfurt)
# ap-southeast-1 → Asia Pacific (Singapore)

# AZ naming: RegionName + letter suffix
# us-east-1a, us-east-1b, us-east-1c, etc.

sections.title: AWS Global Infrastructure
sections.content:
AWS Global Infrastructure extends beyond just Regions and AZs. Local Zones are extensions of a Region placed closer to large population centers, industry, and IT hubs — they allow you to run latency-sensitive applications closer to end users (for example, the us-west-2-lax-1 Local Zone near Los Angeles delivers single-digit millisecond latency for LA-based users). Local Zones support a subset of AWS services, primarily compute, storage, and networking.

AWS Wavelength Zones embed AWS compute and storage within 5G telecom provider networks, enabling mobile edge computing with ultra-low latency (under 10 milliseconds) for applications like real-time gaming, AR/VR, and autonomous vehicles. AWS Outposts bring native AWS services, infrastructure, and operating models to virtually any on-premises facility. With Outposts, you can run EC2, EBS, RDS, ECS, and more in your own data center using the same AWS APIs, making it ideal for workloads with strict data residency requirements or that need extremely low latency to on-premises systems.

For the Developer Associate exam, understand the hierarchy: Global (IAM, Route 53, CloudFront) → Region (S3, DynamoDB, Lambda) → AZ (EC2, RDS, EBS). Some services are truly global and not tied to any Region — IAM users, roles, and policies exist globally. Route 53 is a global DNS service. CloudFront uses the global edge network. Understanding which services are Regional vs global is frequently tested.

sections.title: AWS Management Interfaces
sections.content:
AWS offers multiple ways to interact with its services. The AWS Management Console is a web-based GUI available at console.aws.amazon.com — it is the easiest interface for exploration and one-off tasks, but it is not suitable for automation or repeatable infrastructure. The console provides service-specific dashboards, wizards, and visual tools. For the exam, know that the console supports CloudShell, a browser-based shell pre-authenticated with your IAM credentials.

The AWS CLI (Command Line Interface) is a unified tool to manage AWS services from your terminal. After installing it, you configure it with `aws configure` which prompts for Access Key ID, Secret Access Key, default Region, and output format. Credentials are stored in `~/.aws/credentials` and configuration in `~/.aws/config`. The CLI is essential for scripting, automation, and CI/CD pipelines. The v2 CLI offers improved performance and additional features over v1.

AWS SDKs allow you to interact with AWS services programmatically in your application code. AWS provides SDKs for Java, Python (boto3), Node.js, Go, .NET, Ruby, and others. The Java SDK v2 (software.amazon.awssdk) is a complete rewrite of v1 with an immutable client design, async/non-blocking support, HTTP/2, and a lighter footprint. It follows a builder pattern for constructing requests and uses service-specific clients (S3Client, DynamoDbClient, LambdaClient, etc.). Infrastructure as Code tools like CloudFormation (AWS-native) and Terraform (third-party) allow you to define and provision infrastructure declaratively.
sections.codeExample:
<!-- Maven dependency for AWS Java SDK v2 BOM (Bill of Materials) -->
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId>
      <artifactId>bom</artifactId>
      <version>2.25.0</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId>
    <artifactId>s3</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId>
    <artifactId>sts</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

// Basic S3 list buckets with Java SDK v2
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region;
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.S3Client;
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.ListBucketsResponse;
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.Bucket;

public class S3Example {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // SDK automatically uses IAM role if running on EC2/Lambda
        // or reads from ~/.aws/credentials locally
        S3Client s3 = S3Client.builder()
            .region(Region.US_EAST_1)
            .build();

        ListBucketsResponse response = s3.listBuckets();
        response.buckets().forEach(bucket ->
            System.out.println(bucket.name() + " - " + bucket.creationDate())
        );

        s3.close();
    }
}

# CLI quick reference:
aws configure                          # Set up credentials
aws configure list                     # Show current config
aws sts get-caller-identity            # Verify who you are
aws s3 ls                             # List all buckets
aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket --recursive  # List bucket contents

sections.title: AWS Shared Responsibility Model
sections.content:
The Shared Responsibility Model is one of the most important concepts for any AWS certification exam. AWS is responsible for the security OF the cloud — this means the physical infrastructure, hardware, global network, virtualization layer, and managed service runtimes. Specifically, AWS secures and maintains the physical data centers, networking equipment, hypervisors, and the underlying host operating systems. For managed services like S3, DynamoDB, and Lambda, AWS also patches and maintains the runtime environment.

The customer is responsible for security IN the cloud — everything you deploy and configure on top of AWS infrastructure. For EC2, you are responsible for: patching the guest OS, installing and patching application software, configuring security groups and NACLs, managing IAM users and roles, encrypting data at rest and in transit, and protecting your application credentials. Essentially, if you control it via the AWS console or API, it is your responsibility.

The boundary shifts depending on the service model. For EC2 (IaaS), you manage the most — OS, runtime, application, data, IAM, and network controls. For RDS (managed service), AWS handles the OS and database engine patching, but you are responsible for configuring the DB security group, managing DB users/passwords, enabling encryption, and controlling what data is stored. For Lambda (serverless/PaaS), AWS manages the runtime environment, OS, and hardware — you only manage your function code, IAM execution role, and the data your function processes. This graduated responsibility model means the higher the abstraction level, the less you manage but also the less control you have.

sections.title: IAM Core Concepts
sections.content:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a global service that lets you manage access to AWS services and resources securely. IAM has four main entity types. Users are individual identities created for people or applications that need long-term programmatic or console access — each user has their own credentials. Groups are collections of users that share the same permissions; assigning a policy to a group applies it to all members, making permission management scalable. Roles are identities with policies but no permanent credentials — they are assumed temporarily by AWS services, applications, or users who need them.

The AWS Root Account is created when you first open an AWS account and has complete, unrestricted access to all resources. The root account should never be used for day-to-day work — not even by administrators. Lock it down immediately: enable MFA, delete root access keys, set a billing alarm, and use IAM users for all regular tasks. The root account is required only for a handful of actions like closing the account, changing the account support plan, or restoring an IAM admin if locked out.

The Principle of Least Privilege is foundational to IAM design: grant only the minimum permissions required to perform a task, and nothing more. Start with deny-all, then add the specific permissions needed. Regularly audit and remove unused permissions using IAM Access Advisor (shows last service access dates) and AWS Access Analyzer (flags overly permissive policies). For the exam, remember that users have long-term credentials (access key + secret), roles have short-term temporary credentials issued by STS, and groups cannot be referenced in resource-based policies.
sections.codeExample:
# Create an IAM user
aws iam create-user --user-name alice

# Create a group and add user to it
aws iam create-group --group-name Developers
aws iam add-user-to-group --user-name alice --group-name Developers

# Attach an AWS managed policy to the group
aws iam attach-group-policy \
  --group-name Developers \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess

# Create IAM role for EC2 (trust policy)
aws iam create-role \
  --role-name MyEC2Role \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://ec2-trust-policy.json

# ec2-trust-policy.json:
# {
#   "Version": "2012-10-17",
#   "Statement": [{
#     "Effect": "Allow",
#     "Principal": {"Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com"},
#     "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
#   }]
# }

sections.title: IAM Policies Deep Dive
sections.content:
IAM policies are JSON documents that define permissions. Every policy has a Version (always use "2012-10-17", the current version) and one or more Statement blocks. Each statement has an Effect (Allow or Deny), Action (list of AWS API actions like "s3:GetObject" or "*" for all), Resource (ARN of the resource the action applies to, or "*" for all), and optional Condition (additional restrictions like requiring MFA or limiting source IP).

There are three types of IAM policies by management: AWS Managed policies are pre-built by AWS (e.g., AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess, AdministratorAccess) — they are updated by AWS when new features are released. Customer Managed policies are created and maintained by you — they offer more flexibility and are version-controlled. Inline policies are embedded directly into a single user, group, or role — they are deleted when the identity is deleted and are harder to audit; avoid them unless you specifically need a strict one-to-one relationship.

Policy evaluation follows a strict logic: explicit Deny always wins regardless of any Allow (even an admin Allow cannot override an explicit Deny in a Service Control Policy). If there is no explicit Deny, AWS looks for an explicit Allow. If neither exists, the result is an implicit Deny (default). This three-tier evaluation — explicit deny beats explicit allow beats implicit deny — is tested heavily on the exam. When multiple policies apply (identity policy + resource policy + SCP), AWS evaluates all of them together; an Allow in any source does not override an explicit Deny in any other source.

sections.title: IAM Roles
sections.content:
IAM Roles are the preferred way to grant AWS permissions to EC2 instances, Lambda functions, ECS tasks, and other AWS services — eliminating the need for hardcoded credentials. When you launch an EC2 instance and attach an IAM role (called an Instance Profile), the EC2 metadata service automatically provides temporary, rotating credentials to any application running on that instance. The Java SDK automatically finds these credentials via the DefaultCredentialsProvider chain — you write zero credential-management code.

A role has two components: a Trust Policy (who can assume this role) and a Permissions Policy (what the role can do). The trust policy specifies the Principal — this can be an AWS service (ec2.amazonaws.com for EC2), another AWS account ID for cross-account access, or an identity provider for federated access. The permissions policy is a standard IAM policy document granting the actual AWS actions. When an entity assumes a role, AWS STS issues temporary credentials valid for a configurable duration (15 minutes to 12 hours).

Cross-account access is a powerful pattern: Account A's Lambda function can assume a role in Account B to access that account's resources. The Account B role's trust policy allows Account A's Lambda execution role as a Principal. Account A's Lambda execution role needs permission to call sts:AssumeRole. This eliminates the need to create IAM users in Account B and share long-term credentials. Role chaining (a role assuming another role) is allowed but has limitations — the maximum session duration resets to 1 hour.

sections.title: IAM Best Practices
sections.content:
Following IAM best practices is critical for both production security and passing the exam. Never use the root account for daily operations — create IAM users or use SSO for human access, and use roles for applications. Enable MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) on the root account and on all privileged IAM users. MFA adds a second factor (TOTP app like Google Authenticator, hardware MFA token, or SMS) beyond the username and password.

Access keys for IAM users (programmatic access) should be rotated regularly — 90 days is a common standard. Better yet, prefer roles over access keys wherever possible. For applications running on EC2, Lambda, or ECS, never store access keys in code, configuration files, or environment variables in plaintext — use instance profiles and execution roles instead. For external applications that cannot use AWS roles, store credentials in AWS Secrets Manager or AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (SecureString type) and retrieve them programmatically at runtime.

CloudTrail is your audit trail — it records every API call made in your account (who, what, when, from where). Enable CloudTrail across all regions with a multi-region trail and store logs in an S3 bucket with object lock to prevent tampering. Use IAM Access Analyzer to proactively identify resources shared with external entities. Review IAM Access Advisor reports to identify and remove unused permissions — if a user hasn't used S3 access in 180 days, remove it. Enable AWS Config to continuously audit your IAM configurations against best practice rules.
sections.codeExample:
# Enable MFA for root (must be done in console, not CLI)
# But you CAN check MFA status via CLI:
aws iam get-account-summary | grep MFADevices

# List all IAM users with their last activity
aws iam generate-credential-report
aws iam get-credential-report --query 'Content' --output text | base64 -d

# List access keys and their age
aws iam list-access-keys --user-name alice
aws iam get-access-key-last-used --access-key-id AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE

# Rotate an access key (safe zero-downtime rotation)
# Step 1: Create new key
aws iam create-access-key --user-name alice
# Step 2: Update your app to use the new key
# Step 3: Deactivate (not delete) old key to verify nothing breaks
aws iam update-access-key --user-name alice \
  --access-key-id OLD_KEY_ID --status Inactive
# Step 4: After confirming, delete old key
aws iam delete-access-key --user-name alice --access-key-id OLD_KEY_ID

# Enable CloudTrail (multi-region)
aws cloudtrail create-trail \
  --name MyOrgTrail \
  --s3-bucket-name my-audit-logs-bucket \
  --is-multi-region-trail \
  --enable-log-file-validation
aws cloudtrail start-logging --name MyOrgTrail

sections.title: Security Token Service (STS)
sections.content:
AWS Security Token Service (STS) is the service that issues temporary, limited-privilege credentials for IAM roles and federated users. STS credentials consist of three components: an Access Key ID, a Secret Access Key, and a Session Token. Unlike regular IAM user access keys, STS credentials are time-limited (15 minutes to 36 hours depending on the operation) and automatically expire, significantly reducing the blast radius if credentials are compromised.

The primary STS operations are AssumeRole (for cross-account access and service roles), AssumeRoleWithSAML (for federation with enterprise identity providers like Active Directory or Okta via SAML 2.0), AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (for federation with web identity providers like Amazon Cognito, Google, or Facebook), and GetSessionToken (for existing IAM users who need MFA-validated temporary credentials). When a Lambda function executes, STS automatically provides it with temporary credentials scoped to its execution role — you never see this happening, but it's STS working behind the scenes.

Federation allows external identities (corporate users, app users) to access AWS without having IAM users. SAML 2.0 federation integrates with enterprise identity providers — your AD user can assume an AWS role via SAML assertions without being an IAM user. Web Identity federation using Cognito is the preferred approach for mobile and web app users — Cognito acts as an identity broker, managing the complexity of different social providers and issuing AWS credentials. The exam frequently tests when to use Cognito vs direct web identity federation (always use Cognito for user pools in production).

sections.title: EC2 Fundamentals
sections.content:
Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) provides resizable virtual machines in the cloud, called instances. When you launch an instance, you select an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) — a template containing the OS, pre-installed software, and configuration. AWS provides AMIs for Amazon Linux 2, Amazon Linux 2023, Ubuntu, RHEL, Windows Server, and more. You can also create custom AMIs from existing instances (great for pre-baking your application dependencies) or use AMIs from the AWS Marketplace.

Instance types define the hardware profile of your virtual machine and follow a consistent naming convention: [Family][Generation].[Size]. The family indicates the use case optimization — t for burstable (T3, T4g), m for general purpose (M5, M6i), c for compute-optimized (C5, C6g), r for memory-optimized (R5, R6g), p/g for GPU (P3, G4dn), i/d for storage-optimized (I3, D2). The generation number indicates the hardware generation (higher is newer/better). The size ranges from nano, micro, small, medium, large, xlarge, 2xlarge, up to 48xlarge.

For the exam, know the key families: T-series instances use CPU credits and are burstable — they accumulate credits when idle and spend them when CPU spikes. Standard T instances can't burst beyond baseline if credits run out; T-Unlimited allows sustained bursting at an extra cost. M-series are the workhorse general-purpose instances. C-series are for CPU-intensive workloads (video encoding, scientific modeling). R-series are for in-memory databases and real-time big data. The AWS Graviton (Arm-based) instances (C6g, M6g, R6g) offer up to 40% better price-performance than Intel/AMD equivalents.
sections.codeExample:
# Launch an EC2 instance via CLI
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --key-name MyKeyPair \
  --security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --subnet-id subnet-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=MyEC2InstanceProfile \
  --count 1 \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyApp}]'

# Instance type naming breakdown:
# t3.micro   → t=burstable, 3=3rd gen, micro=2 vCPU, 1GB RAM
# m5.large   → m=general, 5=5th gen, large=2 vCPU, 8GB RAM
# c5.xlarge  → c=compute, 5=5th gen, xlarge=4 vCPU, 8GB RAM
# r5.2xlarge → r=memory, 5=5th gen, 2xlarge=8 vCPU, 64GB RAM
# i3.large   → i=storage optimized (NVMe SSD), 3=3rd gen

# Describe instance types
aws ec2 describe-instance-types \
  --instance-types t3.micro m5.large \
  --query 'InstanceTypes[].{Type:InstanceType,vCPU:VCpuInfo.DefaultVCpus,RAM:MemoryInfo.SizeInMiB}'

sections.title: EC2 Instance Purchasing Options
sections.content:
AWS provides multiple EC2 purchasing models to optimize cost for different workload patterns. On-Demand instances are billed per second (minimum 60 seconds) with no long-term commitments. They are the most expensive per-hour but provide complete flexibility — ideal for unpredictable workloads, development/testing, or applications being run for the first time. There is no capacity guarantee at peak demand, but in practice On-Demand rarely has capacity issues.

Reserved Instances (RIs) provide a significant discount (up to 72%) over On-Demand in exchange for a 1-year or 3-year commitment. Standard RIs give the largest discount but lock you into a specific instance family, region, and size. Convertible RIs offer a slightly smaller discount (~66%) but allow you to change the instance family, OS, and tenancy. RIs are purchased independently of actual instances — they are billing constructs that automatically apply to matching running instances. Savings Plans (Compute and EC2) are the modern, more flexible successor to RIs and can apply across instance families, regions, and even Fargate/Lambda.

Spot Instances allow you to use spare EC2 capacity at up to 90% discount. AWS can reclaim Spot instances with a 2-minute warning when they need the capacity back. Spot is ideal for stateless, fault-tolerant, flexible workloads: batch processing, data analysis, CI/CD, video encoding, and Monte Carlo simulations. Never use Spot for databases, stateful apps, or anything that can't handle interruption. Spot Instance interruption handling: register a handler for the SIGTERM sent 2 minutes before termination to checkpoint your work. Dedicated Hosts provide physical server isolation — required for certain licensing models (Windows Server, SQL Server per-socket licensing) and compliance requirements.

sections.title: EC2 Storage
sections.content:
EC2 instances have two primary storage options. Instance Store (also called ephemeral storage) provides physically attached NVMe SSD storage that offers extremely high IOPS (hundreds of thousands) and low latency because the storage is on the same physical host as your instance. The critical limitation: instance store data is completely lost when the instance is stopped, terminated, or if the underlying hardware fails. Use instance store only for temporary files, buffers, caches, scratch space, or data you replicate across multiple instances.

EBS (Elastic Block Store) volumes are network-attached persistent storage that persists independently of the EC2 instance lifecycle. You can stop, start, and even terminate and re-attach an EBS volume to a new instance. EBS volumes are specific to an AZ — you cannot directly attach an us-east-1a EBS volume to an instance in us-east-1b. EBS volume types: gp3 (general purpose SSD, 3000 IOPS baseline, up to 16000 IOPS, 1000 MB/s throughput, no extra IOPS cost) is the recommended default. gp2 (older, IOPS burst-based, tied to volume size at 3 IOPS/GB, max 16000 IOPS). io1/io2 (Provisioned IOPS SSD, up to 64000 IOPS for io1, 256000 for io2 Block Express) for I/O-intensive databases. st1 (throughput-optimized HDD, max 500 IOPS, 500 MB/s, for big data/log processing). sc1 (cold HDD, max 250 IOPS, lowest cost, for infrequently accessed data).

EBS Snapshots are point-in-time backups stored in S3 (managed by AWS, not visible in your S3). Snapshots are incremental — only changed blocks are saved after the first full snapshot. You can copy snapshots across regions (enabling cross-region DR), share them with other accounts, or use them to create new AMIs. EBS Multi-Attach allows a single io1 or io2 volume to be attached to up to 16 instances in the same AZ simultaneously — the applications must manage concurrent writes (cluster-aware filesystems like GFS2 or application-level locking).

sections.title: EC2 Networking & Security
sections.content:
Security Groups act as virtual firewalls at the ENI (Elastic Network Interface) level. They are stateful — if you allow inbound traffic on port 443, the return traffic is automatically allowed without needing an outbound rule. Security groups contain only allow rules (no deny rules — everything not allowed is implicitly denied). Rules specify protocol, port range, and source/destination (IP CIDR or another security group ID). You can reference another security group as a source — this is how you allow traffic only from instances with a specific SG, regardless of their IP addresses, which is much more dynamic and scalable than IP-based rules.

Network Access Control Lists (NACLs) operate at the subnet level and are stateless — you must explicitly allow both inbound and outbound traffic for any communication. NACLs support both allow and deny rules, evaluated in numerical order (lowest number first). The default NACL allows all traffic; custom NACLs start with deny all. NACLs are the right tool for blocking specific IP addresses (you cannot deny IPs with security groups). Every subnet in a VPC is associated with one NACL (defaults to the VPC's default NACL). A single NACL can be associated with multiple subnets.

Placement Groups control how EC2 instances are distributed across underlying hardware. Cluster placement groups pack instances close together in a single AZ for ultra-low latency and high network throughput (10 Gbps between instances) — ideal for HPC and tightly-coupled parallel computing. Spread placement groups place each instance on distinct hardware racks, reducing the risk of simultaneous failures — ideal for small groups of critical instances (max 7 instances per AZ). Partition placement groups divide instances into logical partitions, each with its own racks and power — ideal for distributed systems like Hadoop, Cassandra, and Kafka where you need to correlate instances (partition-aware replication).

sections.title: EC2 User Data & Metadata
sections.content:
EC2 User Data is a script that runs automatically on first boot of an instance. It runs as root (no sudo needed) and is executed by the cloud-init service. User data is commonly used to bootstrap instances: install packages, download application code, start services, and configure the environment. For Auto Scaling Groups, user data runs on every new instance launched by the group. User data is not re-executed on instance restart by default (only on first launch after launch). The maximum size is 16 KB. You can view and modify user data while the instance is stopped.

EC2 Instance Metadata is data about your running instance accessible from within the instance at the link-local IP address http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/. This includes the instance ID, instance type, AMI ID, public/private IP addresses, security groups, IAM role name, and crucially — the temporary IAM credentials for the attached role (available at /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/RoleName). The metadata service is only accessible from within the EC2 instance itself.

IMDSv2 (Instance Metadata Service version 2) is the current security best practice. Unlike IMDSv1 (simple GET requests), IMDSv2 requires a session-oriented approach — you first make a PUT request to get a session token, then use that token in subsequent metadata requests. This prevents SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) attacks where an attacker tricks your app into fetching metadata. You should enforce IMDSv2 on all instances by setting the HttpTokens metadata option to required. The Java SDK v2 automatically uses IMDSv2 when available.
sections.codeExample:
#!/bin/bash
# EC2 User Data script — install Java 21 and start Spring Boot app
set -e

# Update system packages
yum update -y

# Install Java 21 (Amazon Corretto)
yum install -y java-21-amazon-corretto

# Download application JAR from S3
# (EC2 must have IAM role with S3 read access)
aws s3 cp s3://my-app-bucket/releases/app-1.0.0.jar /opt/app/app.jar

# Create systemd service
cat > /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service << EOF
[Unit]
Description=My Spring Boot App
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=ec2-user
WorkingDirectory=/opt/app
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/app/app.jar
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable myapp
systemctl start myapp

# Fetch metadata (IMDSv2)
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token \
  -H 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600')

# Get instance ID
INSTANCE_ID=$(curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id)

# Get IAM role credentials (automatically rotated by AWS)
ROLE_CREDS=$(curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \
  http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/MyEC2Role)

sections.title: S3 Core Concepts
sections.content:
Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is an object storage service — fundamentally different from block storage (EBS) and file storage (EFS). In object storage, data is stored as objects (files + metadata) in flat containers called buckets. There is no directory hierarchy — what looks like a folder path (images/2024/photo.jpg) is actually the full key of the object. S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) of durability, meaning it automatically stores data redundantly across multiple AZs within a region.

Buckets are containers for objects with globally unique names across all AWS accounts worldwide. Despite being globally named, buckets are created in a specific AWS Region, and data physically stays in that region (unless you configure replication). Bucket names must be between 3-63 characters, lowercase letters/numbers/hyphens only, no underscores, and cannot be formatted as an IP address. Objects have a key (the full path including any prefix), a value (the actual data, up to 5TB per object), metadata (system metadata + user-defined), a version ID (when versioning is enabled), and optional tags.

For objects larger than 100MB, AWS strongly recommends Multipart Upload, and it's required for objects over 5GB. Multipart upload allows you to upload an object in parts simultaneously, then S3 assembles them. This provides better throughput (parallel uploads), the ability to pause and resume, and retry only failed parts rather than the entire file. As of December 2020, S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations — immediately after a PUT or DELETE, any subsequent GET will reflect the change. This replaced the previous eventual consistency model, and the change is frequently referenced in newer exam questions.

sections.title: S3 Storage Classes
sections.content:
S3 offers multiple storage classes with different cost/availability/retrieval-time tradeoffs. S3 Standard is the default — 99.99% availability, 11 nines durability, stored across 3+ AZs, no retrieval fee, suitable for frequently accessed data like active website content, mobile apps, and gaming. It is the most expensive per GB but has no retrieval cost.

S3 Standard-IA (Infrequent Access) is cheaper per GB than Standard but charges a retrieval fee per GB retrieved. It maintains the same multi-AZ redundancy and 11 nines durability. Use it for data accessed a few times per month — disaster recovery backups, older logs. S3 One Zone-IA stores data in only one AZ — 20% cheaper than Standard-IA, but data is lost if the AZ fails. Use for easily re-creatable data or secondary backups you can afford to lose. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between two access tiers (Frequent and Infrequent) based on access patterns with no retrieval fees and a small monitoring/automation fee per object — ideal when access patterns are unknown or unpredictable.

The Glacier family is for archival: Glacier Instant Retrieval provides millisecond retrieval but has a higher retrieval cost than Standard-IA — for quarterly access data like medical images. Glacier Flexible Retrieval (formerly just Glacier) offers retrievals in minutes to hours with three options: Expedited (1-5 min, highest cost), Standard (3-5 hours), and Bulk (5-12 hours, lowest cost). Deep Archive is the cheapest storage ($0.00099/GB/month) but retrieval takes 12-48 hours — for regulatory compliance data you hope to never access. Lifecycle policies automatically transition objects between storage classes based on age (e.g., Standard → Standard-IA after 30 days → Glacier after 90 days → delete after 365 days).

sections.title: S3 Security
sections.content:
S3 security is multi-layered and combines several mechanisms. Bucket Policies are resource-based IAM policies attached directly to the bucket — they can grant or deny access to any principal (AWS account, IAM user, role, or even anonymous public access). They are the primary way to implement cross-account access to S3 without creating IAM users in the owning account. S3 Access Control Lists (ACLs) are a legacy mechanism predating IAM — AWS recommends disabling ACLs entirely for new buckets and using bucket policies instead.

Block Public Access is a set of four independent settings that override any bucket policy or ACL that would make objects public. The four settings are: BlockPublicAcls (new ACLs can't grant public access), IgnorePublicAcls (existing public ACLs are ignored), BlockPublicPolicy (new policies can't grant public access), and RestrictPublicBuckets (restricts access from public IPs even if policy says allow). These settings can be set at the account level (applying to all buckets) or per-bucket. For sensitive data, always enable all four at the account level.

Presigned URLs grant temporary, time-limited access to a specific S3 object — the URL is signed with your IAM credentials and expires after a configurable duration (up to 7 days for SDK-generated URLs). Anyone with the URL can access the object without AWS credentials, regardless of bucket policies. Use presigned URLs to securely share private objects with users, for user uploads that bypass your server (direct browser-to-S3 upload), or for short-lived download links. Server-side encryption options: SSE-S3 (AWS manages keys, AES-256, free, key rotation managed by AWS), SSE-KMS (you control keys via KMS, audit access, additional cost per API call), SSE-C (you provide the encryption key on every request, AWS never stores it), and DSSE-KMS (dual-layer KMS encryption for highest compliance requirements).

sections.title: S3 Advanced Features
sections.content:
S3 Versioning keeps multiple versions of an object in the same bucket. When enabled, every PUT creates a new version with a unique version ID, and deletes are soft-deletes — a delete marker is created but previous versions remain accessible by version ID. Versioning protects against accidental deletion and overwrite. Once enabled, versioning can be suspended but never fully disabled. MFA Delete adds an extra layer of protection by requiring MFA authentication to permanently delete object versions or suspend versioning — only the bucket owner (root account) can enable MFA Delete.

S3 Replication requires versioning to be enabled on both source and destination buckets. Cross-Region Replication (CRR) copies objects to a bucket in a different region — for compliance, lower latency for a geographically distributed team, or disaster recovery. Same-Region Replication (SRR) copies within the same region — for log aggregation across accounts or maintaining a test environment with production data. Replication is asynchronous and does not replicate existing objects (only new objects after replication is configured — use S3 Batch Replication for existing objects). Replication does not replicate delete markers by default (configurable).

S3 Event Notifications send notifications when objects are created, deleted, or restored. Destinations can be Lambda (invoke a function synchronously), SQS (queue the event for async processing), and SNS (fan-out to multiple subscribers). S3 Object Lock implements WORM (Write Once Read Many) storage for compliance: Compliance mode prevents even the root account from deleting objects until the retention period expires — for SEC/FINRA regulated data. Governance mode allows users with special permissions to override the lock. S3 Select allows you to retrieve only the subset of data you need from an object using SQL expressions, reducing the amount of data transferred and query time for large CSV/JSON/Parquet files.

sections.title: S3 Performance & Cost
sections.content:
S3 is designed for high throughput — a single S3 prefix can achieve 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE requests per second and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second. There is no limit to the number of prefixes in a bucket, so performance scales horizontally by distributing objects across multiple prefixes. If you need more than 5,500 GET/s from a single prefix, use CloudFront in front of S3 for caching, or use byte-range fetches to parallelize downloads.

S3 Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront's globally distributed edge network to accelerate uploads and downloads for users far from the S3 bucket's region. Data is uploaded to the nearest CloudFront edge location, which then uses AWS's optimized backbone network to route data to the S3 bucket — speeds can be 50-500% faster for long-distance uploads. There is an additional fee per GB transferred. For very large datasets (TB to PB), consider AWS DataSync (for ongoing file transfer from on-premises NFS/SMB), AWS Snow family (physical devices for offline transfer of 10TB to exabytes), or Direct Connect (for sustained high-volume replication).

S3 pricing has multiple components: storage cost (per GB-month, varies by storage class), request cost (per 1000 PUT/GET operations), data transfer cost (free to S3, free between S3 and EC2 in the same region, $0.09/GB out to the internet), and retrieval fees for IA and Glacier classes. Data Transfer IN to S3 from the internet is always free. Data transfer between S3 and services in the same region via VPC endpoints is also free. S3 Batch Operations allows you to perform bulk operations on billions of objects — copy, restore from Glacier, invoke Lambda, set object tags, modify ACLs — with a single managed job that tracks progress and generates completion reports.

sections.title: Lambda Fundamentals
sections.content:
AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs your code in response to events and automatically manages the underlying compute resources. You provide the code (in a deployment package or container image), define the trigger, and Lambda handles provisioning servers, scaling, patching, and high availability. The key operational model: you pay only for what you use — $0.20 per 1 million invocations plus $0.0000166667 per GB-second of compute time, billed in 1ms increments.

Lambda has hard limits that are critical for architectural decisions: maximum execution timeout of 15 minutes (900 seconds), memory from 128MB to 10,240MB (10GB), with vCPU allocation proportional to memory (at 1,769MB you get one full vCPU, at 3,538MB you get 2 vCPUs). Ephemeral /tmp storage up to 10GB. Deployment package size: 50MB zipped directly, 250MB unzipped (or 10GB for container images). The default concurrent execution limit is 1,000 per region per account (soft limit, can be raised). Each concurrent invocation runs in its own execution environment — there is no shared state between concurrent invocations.

Lambda's execution model has three phases. The Init phase happens when a new execution environment is created — AWS downloads your code, starts the runtime (JVM for Java, Node.js runtime, etc.), and runs your initialization code (static initializers, dependency injection setup). The Invoke phase runs your handler function. AWS reuses warm execution environments across invocations when possible — the container stays alive for several minutes after an invocation, and the next invocation reuses the warm environment (skipping Init), which is critical for Java performance. Understanding the distinction between warm and cold starts directly impacts Java Lambda architecture decisions.

sections.title: Lambda Triggers & Integrations
sections.content:
Lambda integrates with virtually every AWS service as either a trigger or a target. Understanding the invocation model (synchronous vs asynchronous) is critical for designing reliable systems. Synchronous invocations: the caller waits for Lambda to complete and return a response. API Gateway, ALB, Cognito, CloudFront, and direct SDK invocations are synchronous. If Lambda fails, the error is returned to the caller, and the caller must handle retries. There are no automatic retries at the Lambda level for synchronous invocations.

Asynchronous invocations: the caller sends the event to an internal queue and returns immediately (Lambda returns a 202 response). S3 event notifications, SNS, EventBridge, and CloudWatch Events use async invocation. Lambda automatically retries failed async invocations up to 2 times (3 total attempts) with delays between attempts. After all retries fail, the event can be sent to a Dead Letter Queue (SQS or SNS) for further investigation or reprocessing. You can also configure a Lambda Destination — a success destination (where to send the result on success) and a failure destination (where to send on failure), which is more flexible than DLQ.

Event Source Mapping is a Lambda resource that reads from streams and queues and invokes Lambda. Used with: SQS (polls the queue, delivers batches), DynamoDB Streams (reads stream shards), Kinesis Data Streams (reads stream shards), and MSK (Amazon Kafka). For SQS, Lambda polls 5 concurrent long-poll requests, scales up to 60 instances per minute (up to 1000 for standard queues). Failed batches with SQS: by default the entire batch fails and goes back to the queue. Enable bisect-on-error to split the batch and identify specific failing messages. Messages that fail maxReceiveCount times go to the SQS DLQ.

sections.title: Lambda Deployment & Configuration
sections.content:
Lambda functions are deployed as either a ZIP deployment package or a container image (OCI-compliant). ZIP packages must include your compiled code and all dependencies — for Java this means a fat JAR (shaded JAR using the Maven Shade plugin) or an assembly ZIP. You can deploy directly to Lambda (up to 50MB zipped) or upload to S3 first (required for larger packages). Container images up to 10GB give you full control over the runtime environment, pre-warm dependencies, and enable consistent local testing with the same image.

Lambda Layers are separate ZIP archives containing shared code, libraries, or data that multiple functions can reference. Instead of packaging the AWS SDK, common utilities, or large ML models into every function, create a layer and reference it from multiple functions. Layers significantly reduce deployment package sizes, speed up deployments, and centralize shared dependency management. A function can use up to 5 layers, and the total unzipped size (function + all layers) must not exceed 250MB. Layers are immutable — each update creates a new layer version, and functions reference a specific version.

Lambda environment variables are key-value pairs injected into the execution environment — accessible via System.getenv() in Java. They are encrypted at rest using an AWS-managed or customer-managed KMS key. Maximum total size is 4KB. Never store secrets directly in environment variables for sensitive values — instead store the secret ARN in the environment variable and retrieve the actual secret from Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store at runtime. Lambda VPC configuration allows functions to access private resources (RDS, ElastiCache, internal APIs) but introduces cold start latency because Lambda must create an ENI in your VPC's subnet. Use a private subnet with a NAT Gateway if the function also needs internet access.
sections.codeExample:
# Deploy Lambda from JAR
aws lambda create-function \
  --function-name MyJavaFunction \
  --runtime java21 \
  --role arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/LambdaExecutionRole \
  --handler com.example.Handler::handleRequest \
  --code S3Bucket=my-deploy-bucket,S3Key=functions/app-1.0.jar \
  --memory-size 512 \
  --timeout 30 \
  --environment Variables='{DB_SECRET_ARN=arn:aws:secretsmanager:...,REGION=us-east-1}' \
  --tracing-config Mode=Active

# Add a layer
aws lambda publish-layer-version \
  --layer-name CommonUtilities \
  --zip-file fileb://common-utils.zip \
  --compatible-runtimes java21

aws lambda update-function-configuration \
  --function-name MyJavaFunction \
  --layers arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789:layer:CommonUtilities:3

# Configure VPC
aws lambda update-function-configuration \
  --function-name MyJavaFunction \
  --vpc-config SubnetIds=subnet-private-1a,subnet-private-1b,SecurityGroupIds=sg-lambda

# Maven Shade plugin for fat JAR (pom.xml)
// <plugin>
//   <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
//   <artifactId>maven-shade-plugin</artifactId>
//   <configuration>
//     <createDependencyReducedPom>false</createDependencyReducedPom>
//     <shadedArtifactAttached>true</shadedArtifactAttached>
//     <shadedClassifierName>aws</shadedClassifierName>
//   </configuration>
// </plugin>

sections.title: Cold Start & Performance
sections.content:
A Lambda cold start occurs when there is no warm execution environment available to handle an invocation. The cold start sequence has three phases: container initialization (AWS downloads and starts the execution environment — this is AWS's responsibility and is getting faster), runtime initialization (starts the JVM, loads the Java runtime — the most significant factor for Java cold starts), and function initialization (runs your static initializers, Spring context startup, DI framework wiring, and connection pool initialization). For Java, cold starts can range from 1 to 10+ seconds depending on the framework and dependencies.

Provisioned Concurrency is the primary solution to eliminate cold starts entirely. You pre-warm a specific number of execution environments that are always ready to serve requests without initialization delay. Provisioned Concurrency has an additional cost (but you are not charged the normal per-invocation compute cost for those pre-provisioned environments). You can configure it on a function alias or specific version — typically you provision concurrency for your production alias. You can also use Application Auto Scaling to schedule Provisioned Concurrency increases before predictable peak periods.

Lambda SnapStart for Java dramatically reduces cold starts for Java functions. When you publish a function version with SnapStart enabled, Lambda runs the init phase (including your static initializers) and takes a snapshot of the fully initialized memory and disk state. Subsequent cold starts restore from this snapshot instead of re-running initialization, reducing cold start times to under 1 second for most Java applications — even those using Spring Boot or Quarkus. SnapStart requires Java 11 or later (recommended: Java 21) and is available only on published function versions (not $LATEST). Note: you must handle any non-idempotent initialization (random seeds, network connections) using the AfterRestore runtime hook.

sections.title: Lambda Best Practices for Java
sections.content:
Java on Lambda requires deliberate optimization due to the JVM's startup characteristics. Use Java 21 with virtual threads (Project Loom) — virtual threads dramatically improve throughput for I/O-bound Lambda functions by allowing thousands of concurrent operations on a small thread pool. Enable SnapStart on all published versions in production. Minimize your deployment package: only shade the dependencies you actually use, use the AWS SDK v2 (lighter than v1), and exclude unnecessary modules. A bloated 30MB JAR takes much longer to cold-start than a 3MB JAR.

Initialize expensive resources outside the handler method using static initializers — these run during the Init phase and persist across warm invocations. This includes database connection pools, AWS SDK clients, HTTP clients, and Jackson ObjectMapper instances. These objects are shared across concurrent invocations of the same warm container, so they must be thread-safe (which all AWS SDK clients are). Never initialize SDK clients inside the handler method — that would re-create them on every invocation, negating the warm container benefit and wasting the connection setup cost.

For observability, enable AWS X-Ray active tracing to get distributed traces across Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, and other AWS services — X-Ray reveals exactly where time is being spent across your microservices. Use structured logging (JSON) with the Lambda Powertools for Java library, which adds request ID, cold start flag, and correlation IDs automatically. Lambda Power Tuning tool (open-source, runs as a Step Functions state machine) can systematically test different memory configurations to find the optimal balance between cost and performance — often increasing memory from 256MB to 1024MB both speeds up execution and reduces cost because the time savings outweigh the memory cost.

sections.title: DynamoDB Fundamentals
sections.content:
Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless, key-value and document database designed to deliver single-digit millisecond performance at any scale. Unlike relational databases, DynamoDB is schemaless — you define only the key attributes (partition key and optional sort key), and each item can have a different set of non-key attributes. DynamoDB automatically handles replication across 3 AZs within a region, patching, backups, and horizontal scaling — you never interact with the underlying infrastructure.

Every DynamoDB table has a primary key. A simple primary key uses only a Partition Key (also called Hash Key) — the partition key value must be unique across all items in the table. A composite primary key uses a Partition Key + Sort Key (also called Range Key) — the combination must be unique, but multiple items can share the same partition key (as long as sort keys differ). This is powerful for one-to-many relationships: store a user's orders with UserId as partition key and OrderId as sort key — you can fetch all orders for a user in a single efficient query.

DynamoDB supports two data models: key-value (get/put items by primary key) and document (store and query JSON-like nested attributes including lists, maps, and sets). Attribute types include String (S), Number (N), Binary (B), Boolean (BOOL), Null (NULL), List (L), Map (M), String Set (SS), Number Set (NS), and Binary Set (BS). Items can be up to 400KB in size. DynamoDB is not suitable for: complex multi-table JOINs, ad-hoc SQL queries across all data, data normalization, or OLAP analytical queries — use Amazon Redshift or Aurora for those patterns.

sections.title: DynamoDB Read/Write Capacity
sections.content:
DynamoDB offers two capacity modes. In Provisioned mode, you specify the number of Read Capacity Units (RCUs) and Write Capacity Units (WCUs) per second. One RCU provides one strongly consistent read per second (or two eventually consistent reads) for items up to 4KB. One WCU provides one write per second for items up to 1KB. If your item is larger, you need proportionally more capacity units — a 10KB item requires 10 WCUs per write. Auto Scaling can be configured to automatically adjust provisioned capacity based on utilization targets (typically 70% utilization), useful for workloads with predictable but variable traffic.

In On-Demand mode, DynamoDB instantly accommodates your workloads without capacity planning — you pay per request ($1.25 per million writes, $0.25 per million reads in us-east-1). There is no capacity to manage, and the table scales up to previously observed peaks instantly and to new peaks within minutes. On-Demand is ideal for unpredictable workloads, new tables where traffic is unknown, or tables with significant idle periods. The per-request cost is about 6-7x higher than well-utilized Provisioned mode, so switch to Provisioned with auto-scaling once traffic patterns are understood.

Capacity unit math is tested frequently: a 6KB item with strongly consistent reads = 2 RCUs (6KB / 4KB, rounded up = 2). An eventually consistent read of the same item = 1 RCU. A transactional read = 4 RCUs (2x the strongly consistent cost). Writing a 2.5KB item = 3 WCUs (2.5KB / 1KB, rounded up = 3). A transactional write = 6 WCUs (2x). If you provision 100 RCUs, you can handle 100 strongly consistent reads per second of items up to 4KB, or 200 eventually consistent reads per second. ProvisionedThroughputExceededException occurs when you exceed provisioned capacity — implement exponential backoff in your SDK (the Java SDK v2 does this automatically by default).

sections.title: DynamoDB Indexes
sections.content:
Secondary indexes allow you to query on non-primary-key attributes efficiently. Without an index, querying on a non-key attribute requires a Scan (reads the entire table) — expensive and slow for large tables. Local Secondary Indexes (LSIs) share the same partition key as the base table but use a different sort key, enabling alternative sort orders within a partition. LSIs must be defined at table creation and cannot be added later. They share the RCU/WCU capacity with the base table. A table can have up to 5 LSIs, and they are strongly consistent by default (can also be eventually consistent).

Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs) can have any attribute as their partition key and sort key, completely independent of the base table's primary key. GSIs are the primary tool for access pattern flexibility in DynamoDB. Unlike LSIs, GSIs can be created and deleted at any time after table creation. GSIs have their own provisioned capacity (RCU/WCU) independent of the base table — insufficient GSI capacity causes writes to the base table to be throttled (this is a common gotcha). A table can have up to 20 GSIs.

GSI projection determines which attributes are included in the index. KEYS_ONLY projects only the table primary key and index key — smallest index, but you must do a GetItem on the base table if you need other attributes (costs extra RCU). ALL projects all table attributes into the index — largest storage cost but no extra fetches needed. INCLUDE projects specific additional attributes you define. Choosing the right projection is a cost-performance tradeoff: if you always need the same 3-4 attributes with your queries, INCLUDE those attributes and avoid the ALL projection overhead.
sections.codeExample:
// Create a GSI at table creation
aws dynamodb create-table \
  --table-name Orders \
  --attribute-definitions \
      AttributeName=customerId,AttributeType=S \
      AttributeName=orderId,AttributeType=S \
      AttributeName=status,AttributeType=S \
      AttributeName=createdAt,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema \
      AttributeName=customerId,KeyType=HASH \
      AttributeName=orderId,KeyType=RANGE \
  --global-secondary-indexes '[{
    "IndexName": "status-createdAt-index",
    "KeySchema": [
      {"AttributeName": "status", "KeyType": "HASH"},
      {"AttributeName": "createdAt", "KeyType": "RANGE"}
    ],
    "Projection": {"ProjectionType": "INCLUDE",
                   "NonKeyAttributes": ["customerId", "totalAmount"]},
    "ProvisionedThroughput": {"ReadCapacityUnits": 10, "WriteCapacityUnits": 5}
  }]' \
  --billing-mode PROVISIONED \
  --provisioned-throughput ReadCapacityUnits=100,WriteCapacityUnits=50

// Query using GSI in Java SDK v2
QueryResponse response = dynamoDb.query(QueryRequest.builder()
    .tableName("Orders")
    .indexName("status-createdAt-index")
    .keyConditionExpression("#s = :status AND createdAt BETWEEN :start AND :end")
    .expressionAttributeNames(Map.of("#s", "status")) // 'status' is reserved word
    .expressionAttributeValues(Map.of(
        ":status", AttributeValue.fromS("PENDING"),
        ":start", AttributeValue.fromS("2024-01-01"),
        ":end", AttributeValue.fromS("2024-12-31")
    ))
    .build());

sections.title: DynamoDB Queries & Operations
sections.content:
The Query operation retrieves items based on the primary key (required) with an optional sort key condition (begins_with, between, <, >, <=, >=, = operators). Query can also filter results using FilterExpression — important caveat: filter expressions are applied AFTER the query reads items from DynamoDB (RCU charges are based on all items read, not just those returned). This means a filter expression on a non-indexed attribute does not save RCU — use indexes for attributes you frequently filter on. Query results are paginated — if the result set exceeds 1MB, use the LastEvaluatedKey to continue from where you left off.

The Scan operation reads every item in a table or index. Scans are expensive (consume RCU for every item read), slow on large tables, and should be avoided for production query patterns — they indicate a missing index. The only legitimate use cases for Scan are: one-time data exports, administrative tasks, or very small tables. You can use Parallel Scan to speed up table exports by dividing the table into segments and scanning each segment with a separate thread, but this still consumes all available RCU.

Conditional Writes allow you to update or delete items only if certain conditions are met, enabling optimistic locking patterns. The ConditionExpression is evaluated before the write — if it fails, the write is rejected with a ConditionalCheckFailedException. This is how you implement optimistic concurrency: add a version attribute to items, increment it on each write, and include a condition that the current version matches what you read. Transactions (TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems) group up to 100 operations atomically across multiple items and tables — either all succeed or all fail. Transactions cost 2x WCU/RCU. Use transactions for financial operations, inventory management, and any multi-item consistency requirements.

sections.title: DynamoDB Streams & Advanced
sections.content:
DynamoDB Streams provide an ordered, time-stamped log of all item-level changes to a table. Each stream record represents a single item modification (INSERT, MODIFY, REMOVE) and is retained for 24 hours. Stream records can include just the keys, just the new image (item after change), just the old image (item before change), or both old and new images — configured by the StreamViewType. DynamoDB Streams are the foundation for real-time triggers (Lambda), replication, and audit trails. Lambda uses an event source mapping to read from the stream and invoke your function with a batch of records.

Global Tables extend DynamoDB to multiple AWS regions simultaneously, providing multi-master (active-active) replication. Any write to a table in any region is automatically replicated to all other regions within seconds. Global Tables use eventually consistent cross-region replication, so the same item might briefly show different values in different regions if written simultaneously. Use last-writer-wins conflict resolution (built-in) or design your application to avoid simultaneous writes to the same item across regions. Global Tables require DynamoDB Streams to be enabled.

DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, in-memory cache for DynamoDB delivering microsecond read performance (versus single-digit millisecond for DynamoDB). DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB — you swap the DynamoDbClient with a DaxClient, and the cache is transparent. DAX is ideal for read-heavy workloads, gaming leaderboards, real-time bidding, and e-commerce product catalogs. DAX does not help with write-heavy workloads (writes must still hit DynamoDB). TTL (Time to Live) allows you to define an attribute (must be a Unix epoch timestamp Number type) and DynamoDB will automatically delete items when that timestamp is past — no RCU/WCU consumed, great for session data, temporary tokens, and expiring caches.

sections.title: RDS Fundamentals
sections.content:
Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service) is a managed service that makes it easier to set up, operate, and scale relational databases in the cloud. RDS supports six database engines: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, and Amazon Aurora. AWS manages the underlying infrastructure, OS patching, database engine patching, automated backups, and Multi-AZ failover — you manage the database schema, queries, users, and application code.

Automated backups are enabled by default and retained for 1-35 days (default 7 days). Backups occur during a configurable 30-minute backup window and capture the entire DB instance to S3. Point-in-time recovery allows you to restore to any second within the retention period. Transaction logs are backed up every 5 minutes. Manual DB snapshots are user-initiated and retained indefinitely (you must explicitly delete them) — use them before major application upgrades or schema changes.

Multi-AZ deployments provide high availability and automatic failover. AWS maintains a synchronous standby replica in a different AZ. The standby is completely passive — it does not serve reads, it is purely for failover. When a failure is detected (hardware failure, AZ outage, OS crash), AWS automatically updates the DNS endpoint to point to the standby (promotion takes 1-2 minutes). Your application must use the RDS endpoint (not the instance IP) for failover to be transparent. Multi-AZ is for HA (high availability) and disaster recovery, NOT for read scaling — a common exam trap. Failover is also triggered manually when you reboot a Multi-AZ instance with failover.

sections.title: RDS Read Replicas
sections.content:
Read Replicas use asynchronous replication to maintain up to 15 copies of your database that can serve read traffic. Each Read Replica has its own DNS endpoint — your application must be updated to route read queries to the replica endpoint and write queries to the primary endpoint. Read Replicas reduce load on the primary instance for read-heavy workloads (analytics, reporting, BI tools) while the primary handles all writes. Read Replicas can be in the same AZ, different AZ, or even different regions (Cross-Region Read Replicas for global applications or DR purposes).

Replication lag is the delay between a write on the primary and its appearance on the replica — typically sub-second for same-region replicas. Your application must be able to tolerate eventual consistency for data read from replicas. For queries that require the absolute latest data immediately after a write (like showing a user their just-submitted order), route them to the primary. For reports, dashboards, and analytics that can tolerate slightly stale data, use the replica. Some BI tools like AWS QuickSight, Redshift, and Aurora integration let you point directly at a read replica.

A Read Replica can be promoted to become a standalone RDS instance — this breaks replication permanently and the promoted instance becomes independent. This is useful for disaster recovery when the primary fails and you need to promote a replica, or for development (spin up a read replica from production and promote it to get a fresh dev environment with real data). Note: promoting a Read Replica is different from Multi-AZ failover — promotion is a manual operation that changes the replica to a standalone, writable instance. Cross-region Read Replicas have a per-GB data transfer cost for the replication traffic.
sections.codeExample:
# Create a Read Replica
aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica \
  --db-instance-identifier my-mysql-replica \
  --source-db-instance-identifier my-mysql-prod \
  --db-instance-class db.m5.large \
  --availability-zone us-east-1b

# Create a Cross-Region Read Replica
aws rds create-db-instance-read-replica \
  --db-instance-identifier my-mysql-eu-replica \
  --source-db-instance-identifier arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:123456789:db:my-mysql-prod \
  --db-instance-class db.m5.large \
  --region eu-west-1

# Spring Boot — Route reads to replica, writes to primary
# application.yml:
# spring:
#   datasource:
#     primary:
#       url: jdbc:mysql://primary.cluster-xyz.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com:3306/mydb
#       username: admin
#     replica:
#       url: jdbc:mysql://replica.cluster-xyz.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com:3306/mydb
#       username: readonly_user

// Use @Transactional(readOnly = true) on service methods
// that should route to the replica
@Service
public class OrderService {
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)  // Routes to replica
    public List<Order> getOrderHistory(String customerId) { ... }
    
    @Transactional  // Routes to primary
    public Order createOrder(OrderRequest request) { ... }
}

sections.title: Amazon Aurora
sections.content:
Amazon Aurora is AWS's cloud-native relational database engine compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL. Aurora achieves significantly higher performance than standard MySQL (up to 5x) and PostgreSQL (up to 3x) through its custom storage layer. Instead of replicating the entire database, Aurora replicates only the storage-layer redo log, which requires far less I/O. The storage layer is a distributed, fault-tolerant, self-healing SSD-based system that automatically grows from 10GB to 128TB in 10GB increments.

Aurora storage maintains 6 copies of your data across 3 AZs — it can tolerate the loss of 2 copies without losing write availability, and 3 copies without losing read availability. Aurora's cluster endpoint automatically routes writes to the primary instance. The reader endpoint load-balances read queries across all available read replicas. Aurora supports up to 15 low-latency read replicas (vs 5 for RDS) with replica lag typically under 10ms (vs seconds for RDS replicas). Aurora failover is faster than RDS (30 seconds vs 1-2 minutes) because there is no data transfer required — replicas already have access to the same storage.

Aurora Serverless v2 automatically scales database capacity in fine-grained increments (0.5 ACU up to 128 ACUs, where 1 ACU = ~2GB RAM) within seconds based on actual demand. You pay per ACU-second, and it can scale down to near-zero during idle periods (0.5 ACU minimum when configured for serverless). Aurora Global Database spans multiple regions with sub-1-second replication — ideal for globally distributed applications with low-latency reads in each region and disaster recovery with an RPO of under 1 second and RTO of under 1 minute (managed failover).

sections.title: RDS Security
sections.content:
RDS security follows a defense-in-depth approach. Network isolation is the first layer: always deploy RDS instances in private subnets with no direct public internet access. The RDS security group should only allow inbound connections from your application tier's security group (not from 0.0.0.0/0 or specific IP ranges that change). Define a DB subnet group that spans multiple private subnets across AZs, and associate it with your RDS cluster to ensure Multi-AZ failover stays within private subnets.

Encryption at rest uses AWS KMS and must be enabled at DB instance creation — you cannot enable encryption on an existing unencrypted RDS instance after creation (workaround: create a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, restore from the encrypted snapshot). Encrypted RDS instances encrypt the underlying storage, automated backups, Read Replicas, and snapshots using the same KMS key. For encryption in transit, SSL/TLS is supported and should be required — configure it via the rds.force_ssl parameter (for PostgreSQL) or by requiring SSL in your application connection string.

IAM database authentication allows you to use IAM credentials instead of a database password for MySQL and PostgreSQL engines. Your application calls RDS to generate a 15-minute authentication token, then uses that token as the database password. This eliminates database passwords from your code and secrets rotation challenges. To use this pattern, enable IAM auth on the DB instance and grant the IAM role the rds-db:connect permission. In production, combine IAM auth with AWS Secrets Manager (for the master password) with automatic rotation enabled — Secrets Manager can automatically rotate the master RDS password and even the application user passwords.

sections.title: ElastiCache
sections.content:
Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory caching service supporting two engines: Redis and Memcached. Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is feature-rich: it supports complex data structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, hyperloglogs, geospatial indexes), persistence (RDB snapshots and AOF append-only file), pub/sub messaging, Lua scripting, transactions, and cluster mode (automatically sharding data across multiple nodes). ElastiCache for Redis also supports multi-AZ replication with automatic failover. Use Redis for session stores, leaderboards, real-time analytics, rate limiting, pub/sub, and any use case requiring data persistence or complex data types.

Memcached is simpler and faster for basic caching: pure in-memory key-value store, multi-threaded (can fully utilize multiple cores), no persistence, no replication, auto-discovery of nodes, and horizontal scaling by adding nodes. Use Memcached when you need the simplest possible caching layer with maximum throughput for basic string values, and you don't need persistence or replication. The exam typically steers toward Redis unless the question specifically mentions multi-threading or simplicity.

The most common caching patterns are Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) and Write-Through. Cache-Aside: on read, check cache first; if miss, read from database, store in cache, return to caller. Data in cache is always queried data; cache may be stale (set a TTL to limit staleness). Write-Through: on every write to the database, also write to the cache. Cache is always up-to-date but adds latency to writes, and you cache data that may never be read. For session management, store session data in Redis with a TTL equal to the session timeout — sessions survive application instance restarts and work with any load-balanced instance.

sections.title: SQS — Simple Queue Service
sections.content:
Amazon SQS is a fully managed message queuing service that enables decoupling of distributed application components. Producers send messages to a queue; consumers poll the queue and process messages independently. This decoupling provides resilience — if the consumer crashes, messages wait in the queue for up to the message retention period (default 4 days, max 14 days). SQS has two types: Standard queues offer virtually unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery (a message might be delivered more than once), and best-effort ordering. Your consumers must be idempotent to handle duplicate messages.

FIFO (First-In-First-Out) queues guarantee exactly-once processing and strict ordering. FIFO queues process messages in the exact order they are sent, within a Message Group (identified by MessageGroupId). Different Message Groups are processed independently and in parallel. FIFO queue names must end in .fifo. Throughput is limited to 300 messages/second (or 3000 with batching of 10) for the high throughput mode, FIFO queues support up to 3000 TPS.

The Visibility Timeout is the critical operational parameter — when a consumer receives a message, it becomes invisible to other consumers for the duration of the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds, max 12 hours). The consumer must explicitly call DeleteMessage within this window after successful processing. If it doesn't (consumer crashes, takes too long, or forgets), the message becomes visible again and another consumer will receive it. Set the visibility timeout to match your maximum processing time, with some buffer. If processing time is variable, use ChangeMessageVisibility to extend the timeout while processing. For Lambda triggers, Lambda automatically extends visibility timeout if needed and calls DeleteMessage on success.

sections.title: SQS Advanced
sections.content:
The Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) is a separate SQS queue that receives messages that fail processing repeatedly. You configure a redrive policy on the source queue specifying the DLQ ARN and maxReceiveCount (the number of times a message can be received before being moved to DLQ). DLQs are essential for debugging failed messages without losing them — inspect DLQ messages to diagnose poison pills (malformed messages that always fail) or systemic errors. Set DLQ retention period longer than the source queue to ensure you have time to investigate.

Short polling (the default) returns immediately whether or not messages are available, consuming API calls and cost even when the queue is empty. Long polling (recommended) waits up to 20 seconds for a message to arrive before returning an empty response. Long polling significantly reduces cost and empty responses — enable it by setting WaitTimeSeconds to 1-20 on your ReceiveMessage calls, or set the ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds attribute on the queue itself. All production SQS consumers should use long polling.

Delay Queues introduce a delivery delay of 0-900 seconds (15 minutes) before a message becomes visible to consumers — useful for delayed notifications, scheduled processing, or giving downstream systems time to prepare before processing an event. This is different from Visibility Timeout (which hides a message that has already been received). Message Deduplication in FIFO queues uses a deduplication ID (MD5 hash of message body, or your explicit ID) within a 5-minute deduplication window — duplicate messages with the same ID are discarded. This provides exactly-once semantics. For request/response patterns with SQS, use temporary queues (per-client reply queues) — create a unique queue per client session and reference it in the ReplyToQueueUrl message attribute.
sections.codeExample:
# Create SQS queue with DLQ
# First create the DLQ
aws sqs create-queue \
  --queue-name my-app-dlq \
  --attributes '{"MessageRetentionPeriod":"1209600"}' # 14 days

# Get DLQ ARN
DLQ_ARN=$(aws sqs get-queue-attributes \
  --queue-url https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/123456789/my-app-dlq \
  --attribute-names QueueArn \
  --query 'Attributes.QueueArn' --output text)

# Create main queue with DLQ redrive policy + long polling
aws sqs create-queue \
  --queue-name my-app-queue \
  --attributes "{
    \"ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds\": \"20\",
    \"VisibilityTimeout\": \"120\",
    \"MessageRetentionPeriod\": \"345600\",
    \"RedrivePolicy\": \"{\\\"deadLetterTargetArn\\\":\\\"$DLQ_ARN\\\",\\\"maxReceiveCount\\\":\\\"3\\\"}\"
  }"

# Create FIFO queue
aws sqs create-queue \
  --queue-name OrderProcessing.fifo \
  --attributes '{
    "FifoQueue": "true",
    "ContentBasedDeduplication": "true",
    "VisibilityTimeout": "60"
  }'

// Send to FIFO queue (MessageGroupId required)
sqs.sendMessage(r -> r
    .queueUrl(fifoQueueUrl)
    .messageBody(orderJson)
    .messageGroupId("customer-" + customerId)  // All orders for same customer
    .messageDeduplicationId(orderId)  // Idempotent — same ID = duplicate
);

sections.title: SNS — Simple Notification Service
sections.content:
Amazon SNS is a fully managed pub/sub messaging service. Publishers send messages to an SNS Topic; SNS delivers the message to all subscribers of that topic simultaneously. SNS supports multiple subscription protocols: SQS (deliver to queue), Lambda (invoke function), HTTP/HTTPS (POST to endpoint), Email/Email-JSON (send email), SMS (text message), and Mobile Push (APNS, FCM, ADM for iOS/Android). The fan-out pattern — one SNS message delivering to multiple SQS queues — is the most common architecture pattern on the exam.

SNS Message Filtering allows you to subscribe multiple endpoints to one topic but filter which messages each subscriber receives. You set a subscription filter policy (JSON) that specifies attribute conditions. Only messages whose MessageAttributes match the filter policy are delivered to that subscription. This eliminates the need for multiple topics and simplifies your architecture. For example, an order topic with a subscription for the inventory service filtered on eventType=ORDER_CREATED, and another subscription for the shipping service filtered on eventType=ORDER_PAID.

SNS FIFO Topics (SNS.fifo) maintain strict message ordering and provide exactly-once delivery to SQS FIFO queues — critical for financial transactions, inventory updates, and any use case where out-of-order processing causes correctness issues.
