FIFO SNS topics can only fan out to SQS FIFO queues. Throughput is limited to 300 messages/second per topic (3000 with batching). For message durability, always fan-out through SQS — direct Lambda subscriptions have no built-in retry for delivery failures (the message is lost if Lambda returns an error), whereas SQS queues buffer messages until Lambda successfully processes them.
sections.codeExample:
// Create SNS topic and fan-out to multiple SQS queues
# Create SNS topic
TOPIC_ARN=$(aws sns create-topic --name OrderEvents --query TopicArn --output text)

# Create SQS queues for each downstream service
for SERVICE in inventory email analytics fraud shipping; do
  QUEUE_URL=$(aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders-${SERVICE} --query QueueUrl --output text)
  QUEUE_ARN=$(aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url $QUEUE_URL \
    --attribute-names QueueArn --query 'Attributes.QueueArn' --output text)
  
  # Allow SNS to write to this SQS queue
  aws sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url $QUEUE_URL --attributes "{
    \"Policy\": \"{\\\"Statement\\\":[{\\\"Effect\\\":\\\"Allow\\\",
    \\\"Principal\\\":{\\\"Service\\\":\\\"sns.amazonaws.com\\\"},
    \\\"Action\\\":\\\"sqs:SendMessage\\\",
    \\\"Resource\\\":\\\"$QUEUE_ARN\\\",
    \\\"Condition\\\":{\\\"ArnEquals\\\":{\\\"aws:SourceArn\\\":\\\"$TOPIC_ARN\\\"}}}]}\""
  
  # Subscribe SQS queue to SNS topic with filter
  aws sns subscribe \
    --topic-arn $TOPIC_ARN \
    --protocol sqs \
    --notification-endpoint $QUEUE_ARN \
    --attributes FilterPolicy='{"eventType":["ORDER_CREATED","ORDER_PAID"]}'
done

// Java SDK v2 — publish to SNS with message attributes
SnsClient sns = SnsClient.builder().region(Region.US_EAST_1).build();

sns.publish(r -> r
    .topicArn("arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789:OrderEvents")
    .message("{\"orderId\":\"o-123\",\"amount\":99.99}")
    .messageAttributes(Map.of(
        "eventType", software.amazon.awssdk.services.sns.model
            .MessageAttributeValue.builder()
            .stringValue("ORDER_CREATED").dataType("String").build()
    ))
);

sections.title: Amazon EventBridge
sections.content:
Amazon EventBridge (formerly CloudWatch Events) is a serverless event bus that makes it easy to build event-driven architectures. The default event bus receives events from AWS services automatically — EC2 state changes, S3 object creation, IAM changes, RDS events, and hundreds of other AWS service events. You create Rules on the event bus that match specific event patterns and route matching events to targets. One rule can have up to 5 targets. Targets include Lambda, SQS, SNS, ECS tasks, Step Functions, Kinesis, API Gateway, and more.

Custom event buses allow you to receive events from your own applications using the PutEvents API. This is the foundation for an event-driven microservices architecture where services emit business events (OrderCreated, PaymentProcessed, InventoryUpdated) to the custom bus, and other services subscribe to the events they care about. The schema registry automatically discovers event schemas from your event buses, generates code bindings in Java, Python, and TypeScript, and allows you to validate events against schemas in your CI/CD pipeline.

Scheduled Rules allow you to invoke targets on a recurring schedule using either a rate expression (rate(5 minutes), rate(1 hour), rate(7 days)) or a cron expression (cron(0 12 * * ? *) for noon UTC daily). This replaces the need for dedicated scheduling infrastructure and is the recommended way to trigger Lambda for batch jobs, cleanup tasks, and report generation. Partner Event Sources allow you to receive events directly from SaaS providers (Zendesk, Shopify, Datadog, PagerDuty, Stripe) into a partner event bus without polling or custom integration code.

sections.title: Messaging Patterns for Exam
sections.content:
Understanding when to use SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge vs Kinesis is critical for the Developer Associate exam. Use SQS when you need a reliable queue to decouple a producer from a consumer, handle traffic spikes by buffering messages, ensure messages are not lost if the consumer is down, or implement work queues for distributed processing. SQS is pull-based — consumers poll for messages. Use SNS when you need to deliver a single event to multiple subscribers simultaneously (fan-out), send notifications to multiple protocols (email, SMS, HTTP), or broadcast events where you don't need delivery guarantees beyond SNS's own retry logic.

The SNS + SQS fan-out pattern is one of the most commonly tested patterns: publish once to SNS, which automatically delivers to multiple SQS queues — each queue feeds an independent consumer (Lambda or EC2). This decouples publishers from subscribers, allows each subscriber to scale independently, provides durability (SQS buffers if subscriber is slow), and allows adding new subscribers without modifying the publisher. EventBridge is preferred over SNS for event-driven architectures within AWS — it understands AWS service event formats, supports content-based filtering, has the schema registry, and routes to more target types.

Kinesis Data Streams is for when you need to process high-volume streaming data (millions of events/second), maintain ordering within a shard (like FIFO but at massive scale), replay events (records stored for 24 hours to 7 days), or have multiple independent consumers reading the same stream at their own pace. Key difference: SQS messages are consumed and deleted; Kinesis records can be replayed. Use Kinesis for clickstream analysis, real-time metrics, IoT telemetry, log aggregation, and stock market feeds. The exam often contrasts SQS (queue, delete on consume) vs Kinesis (stream, replay, multiple consumers).

sections.title: VPC Fundamentals
sections.content:
Amazon VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is your private, logically isolated section of the AWS cloud where you launch resources in a virtual network that you define. You have complete control over your virtual networking environment: IP address range selection (CIDR blocks), subnet creation, route table configuration, and network gateway setup. A VPC spans all AZs within a Region. The maximum CIDR block for a VPC is /16 (65,536 IP addresses); the minimum is /28 (16 IP addresses). You can add up to 4 additional CIDR blocks to an existing VPC.

Subnets divide your VPC into segments, each within a single AZ. A public subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway (IGW) in its route table, allowing instances to have public IPs and communicate with the internet. A private subnet has no route to an IGW — instances cannot receive inbound connections from the internet. Within a subnet, AWS reserves 5 IP addresses (first 4 and last) for internal purposes: the network address, VPC router, DNS server, future use, and broadcast address. So a /24 subnet (256 addresses) gives you 251 usable IPs.

The Default VPC is automatically created in every AWS Region when you create an account. It has a /16 CIDR (172.31.0.0/16), subnets in every AZ, an Internet Gateway attached, and all subnets configured as public (default route to IGW). The Default VPC is designed for ease of getting started but should not be used for production workloads — it lacks private subnets, and all instances get public IPs by default. For production, create a custom VPC with a proper architecture: public subnets for load balancers, private subnets for application servers, and isolated subnets for databases.

sections.title: Internet Gateway, NAT & Routing
sections.content:
An Internet Gateway (IGW) is a horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC component that allows communication between your VPC and the internet. It performs Network Address Translation (NAT) for instances with public IP addresses — translating private IPs to the instance's public IP for outbound traffic, and the reverse for inbound. An IGW is attached to a VPC (one IGW per VPC) and is fully managed by AWS — there is no bandwidth bottleneck or availability concern. For an instance to be reachable from the internet, it must: be in a public subnet, have a public IP or Elastic IP, and have a security group allowing the desired inbound traffic.

NAT Gateway allows instances in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet (for software updates, API calls) while preventing the internet from initiating connections to those instances. A NAT Gateway must be deployed in a public subnet and requires an Elastic IP address. For high availability, deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ — if you share a single NAT Gateway across AZs, an AZ failure will cut off internet access for all private instances in other AZs. NAT Gateways are AWS-managed (no patching required, auto-scale up to 100 Gbps) and cost $0.045/hr plus $0.045/GB of data processed.

Route Tables control where network traffic is directed. Each VPC has a main route table (applied to subnets not explicitly associated with another route table). For a public subnet route table: the local route (10.0.0.0/16 → local) for VPC-internal traffic, and 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxx for all internet traffic. For a private subnet route table: 10.0.0.0/16 → local, and 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxx for NAT Gateway. The most specific route (longest prefix match) wins — a route to 10.0.5.0/24 takes precedence over 10.0.0.0/16 for matching traffic.
sections.codeExample:
# Complete VPC setup with public/private subnets + NAT
# 1. Create and attach IGW
IGW_ID=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId --output text)
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id $IGW_ID --vpc-id $VPC_ID

# 2. Create Elastic IP and NAT Gateway (in public subnet)
ALLOC_ID=$(aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc --query AllocationId --output text)
NAT_ID=$(aws ec2 create-nat-gateway \
  --subnet-id $PUBLIC_SUBNET_ID \
  --allocation-id $ALLOC_ID \
  --query NatGateway.NatGatewayId --output text)

# 3. Configure public subnet route table
PUBLIC_RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $PUBLIC_RT \
  --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id $IGW_ID
aws ec2 associate-route-table --subnet-id $PUBLIC_SUBNET_ID --route-table-id $PUBLIC_RT

# 4. Configure private subnet route table
PRIVATE_RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $PRIVATE_RT \
  --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --nat-gateway-id $NAT_ID
aws ec2 associate-route-table --subnet-id $PRIVATE_SUBNET_ID --route-table-id $PRIVATE_RT

# 5. Enable auto-assign public IPv4 for public subnet
aws ec2 modify-subnet-attribute \
  --subnet-id $PUBLIC_SUBNET_ID --map-public-ip-on-launch

sections.title: Security Groups vs NACLs
sections.content:
Security Groups and NACLs (Network Access Control Lists) are both used to control traffic, but they operate at different layers and have distinct behaviors that make them complementary rather than redundant. Security Groups are associated with network interfaces (ENIs) attached to EC2 instances, Lambda (VPC), RDS, ECS tasks, and other services. They are stateful — AWS automatically allows the return traffic for any allowed connection without needing a separate outbound rule. For example, if you allow inbound TCP 443, the outbound response traffic is automatically allowed.

NACLs operate at the subnet boundary and are evaluated for all traffic entering or leaving the subnet. Unlike security groups, NACLs are stateless — you must explicitly allow both inbound and outbound traffic for any communication. If you allow inbound TCP 443, you must also allow the ephemeral outbound ports (1024-65535) for the response. NACLs support both allow and deny rules evaluated in ascending rule number order (100 before 200 before 300). The first matching rule applies — if rule 100 allows and rule 200 denies the same traffic, rule 100 applies. There is an implicit DENY * at the end.

The practical guidance: use Security Groups as your primary firewall for EC2 instances, RDS, Lambda, ECS — they are easier to manage and stateful. Use NACLs as an additional subnet-level defense when you need to block specific IP addresses or IP ranges (for example, blocking a known malicious IP). You cannot create a Deny rule in a Security Group — if you need to explicitly block traffic from a specific IP while allowing all others, you need a NACL. In practice, most architectures rely primarily on Security Groups and use NACLs only for specific network-level blocking.
sections.codeExample:
// Security Groups vs NACLs — Side-by-Side Comparison:
//
// SECURITY GROUP:              NACL:
// Applied to: ENI/instance     Subnet level (all instances)
// Stateful: YES                Stateful: NO
// Rules: Allow ONLY           Rules: Allow AND Deny
// Evaluation: All rules       Evaluation: In order, first match wins
// Return traffic: Auto        Return traffic: Must explicitly allow
// Default (new): Deny all in  Default NACL: Allow all in/out
//               Allow all out Custom NACL: Deny all in/out

# Example: NACL to block malicious IP
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry \
  --network-acl-id acl-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --rule-number 50 \
  --protocol -1 \
  --rule-action deny \
  --cidr-block 203.0.113.25/32 \
  --ingress  # Deny inbound from this IP

aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry \
  --network-acl-id acl-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --rule-number 100 \
  --protocol tcp \
  --rule-action allow \
  --port-range From=443,To=443 \
  --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 \
  --ingress  # Allow HTTPS from everyone else

# Allow ephemeral ports for return traffic (NACL stateless requirement)
aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry \
  --network-acl-id acl-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --rule-number 100 \
  --protocol tcp \
  --rule-action allow \
  --port-range From=1024,To=65535 \
  --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 \
  --egress  # Return traffic for inbound connections

sections.title: VPC Peering & Private Connectivity
sections.content:
VPC Peering creates a direct network connection between two VPCs, allowing resources in each VPC to communicate using private IP addresses as if they were in the same network. VPC Peering is non-transitive — if VPC A is peered with VPC B, and VPC B is peered with VPC C, VPC A cannot communicate with VPC C through VPC B. Each pair needs its own peering connection. VPC Peering works across different AWS accounts and across regions (inter-region VPC peering) with an additional data transfer charge. There cannot be overlapping CIDR blocks between peered VPCs.

VPC Endpoints enable private connectivity from your VPC to supported AWS services without requiring an Internet Gateway, NAT device, VPN, or Direct Connect connection. Traffic stays on the AWS network. Gateway Endpoints support only S3 and DynamoDB — they are free and work by adding an entry to your route table. Interface Endpoints (powered by AWS PrivateLink) support most other AWS services (SQS, SNS, Lambda, SSM, Secrets Manager, KMS, CloudWatch, etc.) — they create an ENI in your subnet with a private IP address, cost $0.01/hr per AZ, and support security groups.

AWS Transit Gateway is a network transit hub that connects VPCs and on-premises networks through a central hub. Instead of creating a mesh of peering connections between N VPCs (which requires N*(N-1)/2 peering connections), Transit Gateway provides a hub-and-spoke model where each VPC connects to the Transit Gateway once. Transit Gateway supports up to 5,000 VPC attachments, transitive routing (traffic can flow A→TGW→B→TGW→C), route tables per attachment for traffic segmentation, and multi-region support. It is the recommended solution for connecting more than 3-4 VPCs.
sections.codeExample:

sections.title: VPN & Direct Connect
sections.content:
AWS Site-to-Site VPN creates an encrypted IPSec tunnel over the public internet between your on-premises network and your AWS VPC. The AWS side uses a Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) attached to your VPC. The on-premises side uses a Customer Gateway (CGW) — a software or hardware device that you configure. AWS provides two redundant VPN tunnels per connection (in different AZs) for redundancy — if one tunnel fails, traffic automatically fails over to the other. VPN throughput is limited to approximately 1.25 Gbps per connection. VPN is the quickest and cheapest way to establish private connectivity between on-premises and AWS, but it's subject to internet latency and variability.

AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated private network connection between your premises and AWS via a Direct Connect location (a colocation facility). Available in 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, and 100 Gbps ports. Direct Connect offers consistent, predictable low latency (much lower than VPN over internet), higher bandwidth for large data transfers, and reduced data transfer costs compared to internet. However, it takes weeks to months to provision, costs significantly more, and the connection itself is not encrypted by default — the circuit is private but not encrypted. To encrypt over Direct Connect, configure a VPN over the Direct Connect connection (create a Site-to-Site VPN but route it over Direct Connect instead of internet).

For the exam, the key decision criteria: if you need encryption, use VPN (Direct Connect alone is not encrypted). If you need dedicated bandwidth and low latency (e.g., migrating petabytes of data or running latency-sensitive financial applications), use Direct Connect. If you need both low latency/high bandwidth AND encryption, use Direct Connect + VPN. If you need redundancy for Direct Connect, configure two Direct Connect connections to different Direct Connect locations, or pair Direct Connect with a VPN as a backup path.

sections.title: CloudFormation
sections.content:
AWS CloudFormation enables Infrastructure as Code (IaC) — you describe your entire infrastructure in a template (YAML or JSON), and CloudFormation provisions and manages those resources as a Stack. The key benefits over manual provisioning: repeatability (same template creates identical environments in dev/staging/prod), version control (templates in Git = audit trail of infrastructure changes), automatic rollback (if a stack update fails, CloudFormation reverts all changes in the stack), and drift detection (CloudFormation can identify resources that have been manually modified outside of CloudFormation).

A CloudFormation template has sections: AWSTemplateFormatVersion (always 2010-09-09), Description (optional text description), Parameters (input values, referenced with !Ref, allow templates to be reusable across environments), Mappings (static lookup tables, e.g., AMI IDs per region), Conditions (conditional resource creation, e.g., only create CloudFront in production), Resources (required — the AWS resources to create), and Outputs (values to export, referenced by other stacks or the console). Resources use the format Type: AWS::Service::ResourceType (e.g., AWS::S3::Bucket, AWS::Lambda::Function, AWS::EC2::Instance).

Change Sets allow you to preview what changes a template update will make before actually applying them — showing what resources will be added, modified, or deleted. This is critical for production stacks where unexpected resource replacement (deletion + recreation) can cause downtime. CloudFormation Stack Exports and Fn::ImportValue enable cross-stack references — Stack A exports a VPC ID, and Stack B imports it. This allows you to organize large infrastructure into smaller, independently manageable stacks with clear dependencies. Nested Stacks decompose a complex architecture into reusable, modular child stacks referenced from a parent stack.
sections.codeExample:
# CloudFormation YAML — S3 bucket with versioning + Lambda + S3 event
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: S3 upload processor with Lambda

Parameters:
  Environment:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, staging, prod]
    Default: dev

Conditions:
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Environment, prod]

Resources:
  UploadBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'my-uploads-${Environment}-${AWS::AccountId}'
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      NotificationConfiguration:
        LambdaConfigurations:
          - Event: 's3:ObjectCreated:*'
            Filter:
              S3Key:
                Rules:
                  - Name: prefix
                    Value: uploads/
            Function: !GetAtt ProcessorFunction.Arn

  ProcessorFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !Sub 'file-processor-${Environment}'
      Runtime: java21
      Handler: com.example.ProcessorHandler::handleRequest
      Role: !GetAtt LambdaExecutionRole.Arn
      MemorySize: !If [IsProd, 1024, 256]
      Timeout: 60
      SnapStart:
        ApplyOn: PublishedVersions
      Code:
        S3Bucket: my-deployment-bucket
        S3Key: processor-1.0.jar

  LambdaPermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Properties:
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      FunctionName: !GetAtt ProcessorFunction.Arn
      Principal: s3.amazonaws.com
      SourceArn: !GetAtt UploadBucket.Arn

  LambdaExecutionRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: {Service: lambda.amazonaws.com}
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: S3ReadPolicy
          PolicyDocument:
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: [s3:GetObject, s3:GetObjectVersion]
                Resource: !Sub '${UploadBucket.Arn}/*'

Outputs:
  BucketName:
    Value: !Ref UploadBucket
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${Environment}-UploadBucket'

sections.title: CloudWatch
sections.content:
Amazon CloudWatch is the AWS monitoring and observability service. CloudWatch Metrics are numerical data points published by AWS services and your applications. EC2 instances publish default metrics every 5 minutes (CPU, network, disk) — enable detailed monitoring for 1-minute intervals (additional cost). Custom metrics allow you to publish application-specific data (business KPIs, application-level metrics) using the PutMetricData API or CloudWatch Agent. Metrics are organized by namespace (e.g., AWS/EC2), dimensions (key-value pairs like InstanceId), and metric name. Metrics are retained for 15 months at decreasing resolution (1-min for 15 days, 5-min for 63 days, 1-hr for 455 days).

CloudWatch Alarms monitor a single metric and perform actions when the metric crosses a threshold. Alarms have three states: OK, ALARM, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA. Actions can include: publishing to SNS (triggering notifications or Lambda), triggering Auto Scaling Group policies, or performing EC2 actions (stop, terminate, reboot, recover). Composite Alarms evaluate the state of multiple alarms using AND/OR logic — useful for reducing alarm noise (only alert when BOTH CPU is high AND memory is high, not just one). CloudWatch Logs accepts log data from Lambda (automatically), EC2 (via CloudWatch Agent), ECS, API Gateway, and more. Logs are organized into Log Groups (typically one per application/service) and Log Streams (one per instance/invocation).

AWS X-Ray provides distributed tracing for your applications. It generates a service map showing all services and their dependencies, traces individual requests across microservices (including Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, and external HTTP calls), and identifies bottlenecks and errors. The X-Ray SDK instruments your application code — for Java Spring Boot, the X-Ray Spring integration auto-instruments incoming requests and outgoing AWS SDK calls. The exam tests CloudWatch for metrics/logs/alarms and X-Ray for distributed tracing — they are complementary: CloudWatch shows what is happening aggregately, X-Ray shows what is happening for individual requests.
sections.codeExample:
// CloudWatch custom metric from Java
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.cloudwatch.CloudWatchClient;
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.cloudwatch.model.*;

CloudWatchClient cw = CloudWatchClient.builder().region(Region.US_EAST_1).build();

// Publish custom business metric
cw.putMetricData(r -> r
    .namespace("MyApp/Orders")
    .metricData(
        MetricDatum.builder()
            .metricName("OrdersProcessed")
            .value(1.0)
            .unit(StandardUnit.COUNT)
            .dimensions(
                Dimension.builder().name("Environment").value("prod").build(),
                Dimension.builder().name("Region").value("us-east-1").build()
            )
            .build()
    )
);

# Create CloudWatch Alarm
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name HighCPUAlarm \
  --alarm-description "CPU above 80% for 5 minutes" \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --dimensions Name=AutoScalingGroupName,Value=my-asg \
  --statistic Average \
  --period 300 \
  --threshold 80 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --evaluation-periods 2 \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789:AlertsTopic \
  --ok-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789:AlertsTopic

# CloudWatch Logs Insights query (last 1 hour errors)
aws logs start-query \
  --log-group-name /aws/lambda/my-function \
  --start-time $(date -d '1 hour ago' +%s) \
  --end-time $(date +%s) \
  --query-string 'filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count() by bin(5m)'

sections.title: API Gateway
sections.content:
Amazon API Gateway is a fully managed service for creating, publishing, and securing REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs at any scale. REST APIs offer the most features — usage plans (throttle and quota customers by API key), request/response transformation (mapping templates using Velocity Template Language), API caching (reduce latency and backend load), resource-based policies, and AWS WAF integration. HTTP APIs are a newer, simpler, faster, and cheaper (approximately 70% less) option with native support for OIDC/JWT authorizers, automatic CORS support, and lower latency — they lack REST API features like usage plans, request transformation, and API keys.

API Gateway deployment requires deploying to a Stage — stages represent environments (dev, staging, prod) and have their own URLs (https://api-id.execute-api.region.amazonaws.com/stage-name). Stage variables act like environment variables for the stage, allowing you to reference different backend endpoints per stage without changing your API definition. Canary deployments route a percentage of traffic to a new deployment while keeping the rest on the existing version — essential for safe API updates. API Gateway throttles at 10,000 RPS (requests per second) burst and 5,000 RPS steady state at the account level — you can request limit increases.

Integration types: Lambda Proxy integration passes the full request (headers, query params, body, path) to Lambda and returns Lambda's response directly — the simplest and most common integration. HTTP/HTTP_Proxy integration forwards requests to HTTP backends. AWS Service integration allows API Gateway to call AWS services directly (put to SQS, start Step Functions execution) without a Lambda intermediary. WebSocket API maintains persistent connections, routes incoming messages based on a route selection expression, and enables real-time two-way communication for chat, gaming, financial tickers, and collaborative editing.
sections.codeExample:
# Create a simple HTTP API with Lambda integration
APIID=$(aws apigatewayv2 create-api \
  --name MyTodoAPI \
  --protocol-type HTTP \
  --cors-configuration AllowOrigins='*',AllowMethods='GET,POST,DELETE' \
  --query ApiId --output text)

# Create Lambda integration
INTEGRATION_ID=$(aws apigatewayv2 create-integration \
  --api-id $APIID \
  --integration-type AWS_PROXY \
  --integration-uri arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789:function:TodoHandler \
  --payload-format-version 2.0 \
  --query IntegrationId --output text)

# Create routes
aws apigatewayv2 create-route \
  --api-id $APIID \
  --route-key 'GET /todos' \
  --target integrations/$INTEGRATION_ID

aws apigatewayv2 create-route \
  --api-id $APIID \
  --route-key 'POST /todos' \
  --target integrations/$INTEGRATION_ID

aws apigatewayv2 create-route \
  --api-id $APIID \
  --route-key 'DELETE /todos/{id}' \
  --target integrations/$INTEGRATION_ID

# Deploy to prod stage
aws apigatewayv2 create-stage \
  --api-id $APIID \
  --stage-name prod \
  --auto-deploy

# API URL: https://$APIID.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod

// Common 502 Bad Gateway from API Gateway:
// → Lambda function returned an invalid response format
// → Lambda function timed out (check CloudWatch logs)
// → Lambda function threw unhandled exception
// Solution: Check CloudWatch Logs for /aws/apigateway/access_logs
//            and /aws/lambda/your-function

sections.title: Elastic Beanstalk & ECS/EKS
sections.content:
AWS Elastic Beanstalk is a PaaS offering where you deploy your application code (Java WAR, Spring Boot JAR, Node.js app, Python app, etc.) and Beanstalk automatically handles the underlying infrastructure — provisioning EC2 instances, an Application Load Balancer, an Auto Scaling Group, CloudWatch monitoring, and optionally an RDS database. Beanstalk is ideal for developers who want to focus on application code without deep AWS infrastructure knowledge. Beanstalk supports multiple deployment policies: All at once (fastest but causes downtime), Rolling (replaces a batch at a time), Rolling with additional batch (launches new instances first, preventing capacity reduction), Immutable (launches an entirely new set of instances, then swaps), and Blue/Green (using environment SWAP feature — separate URL swap with Route 53 CNAME).

Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) is a fully managed container orchestration service. You define Task Definitions (blueprints specifying Docker image, CPU, memory, networking mode, IAM task role) and run them as Tasks (one-off) or Services (long-running, maintain desired count, integrated with ALB). ECS supports two launch types: Fargate (serverless containers — you specify CPU/memory, AWS manages the underlying EC2, you pay per vCPU-hour and GB-hour) and EC2 (you manage EC2 instances in a cluster, ECS schedules containers on them — more control, potentially cheaper for consistent high utilization). ECS is ideal for microservices, web applications, batch processing, and CI/CD pipelines with Docker.

Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) is a managed Kubernetes control plane — AWS manages the Kubernetes API servers and etcd, you manage the worker nodes (or use Fargate). Use EKS when you are already using Kubernetes and want to avoid managing the control plane, when you need Kubernetes-specific features (Helm, operators, CRDs), or when you're migrating an on-premises Kubernetes workload to AWS. The overhead of Kubernetes (YAML manifests, Helm charts, pod/service/deployment concepts) means EKS has a significantly higher operational complexity than ECS — the exam expects you to choose ECS for greenfield container workloads and EKS when Kubernetes is already in use.
sections.codeExample:
# Deploy Spring Boot app to Elastic Beanstalk
# Initialize Beanstalk application
eb init my-spring-app \
  --platform "Corretto 21 running on 64bit Amazon Linux 2023" \
  --region us-east-1

# Create environment with ALB + Auto Scaling
eb create production-env \
  --instance-type t3.medium \
  --min-instances 2 \
  --max-instances 10 \
  --elb-type application

# Deploy new version
eb deploy production-env

# ECS Fargate — create task definition (simplified)
aws ecs register-task-definition --cli-input-json '{
  "family": "my-java-app",
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "cpu": "512",
  "memory": "1024",
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole",
  "taskRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/myAppTaskRole",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "my-java-app",
    "image": "123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-app:latest",
    "portMappings": [{"containerPort": 8080, "protocol": "tcp"}],
    "logConfiguration": {
      "logDriver": "awslogs",
      "options": {
        "awslogs-group": "/ecs/my-java-app",
        "awslogs-region": "us-east-1",
        "awslogs-stream-prefix": "ecs"
      }
    }
  }]
}'

sections.title: Developer Exam Tips & Common Gotchas
sections.content:
The AWS Developer Associate exam focuses heavily on scenario-based questions requiring you to choose the right service or configuration. Several topics are consistently tested. SQS vs SNS vs Kinesis: SQS for decoupling point-to-point, SNS for fan-out pub/sub, Kinesis for ordered streaming at scale with replay capability. A key differentiator: Kinesis maintains order per shard, SQS FIFO maintains order per MessageGroupId, and SNS has no ordering (except SNS FIFO). For streaming analytics, use Kinesis. For microservice event notification, use SNS+SQS. For simple queue decoupling, use SQS.

Common IAM exam gotchas: explicit Deny always wins (remember: Deny > Allow > implicit Deny). IAM roles for EC2 use instance profiles — never hardcode credentials. When a user assumes a role, their original permissions are replaced by the role's permissions (permissions do not accumulate). An IAM policy that has no effect means the resource-based policy and identity policy must both allow the action (or one allows and the other is absent, but neither explicitly denies). SCP in AWS Organizations can restrict even the root user of an account — if an SCP denies an action, no one in that account can perform it.

Networking exam traps: CORS errors when calling S3 from a browser — configure S3 bucket CORS rules. 502 from ALB usually means the target (Lambda/ECS) returned an invalid response or timed out. Security groups are stateful (no return traffic rule needed), NACLs are stateless (must allow return traffic). S3 strong consistency since December 2020 — no more eventual consistency for S3 reads after writes. Lambda in a VPC needs NAT Gateway for internet access and VPC Endpoints for AWS service access without internet. RDS Multi-AZ is not a read scaling solution — the standby does not serve read traffic. Always check if the question says 'high availability' (Multi-AZ) vs 'read performance' (Read Replicas).
